hints: Notice the vertical axis is velocity, a vector, so motion back down the original path must appear on the opposite side of the time axis from motion up.
Connect the slope of a velocity-time graph to acceleration: the component of weight down the ramp is almost constant, so acceleration down the ramp is constant.
Check what happens at the highest point: velocity must pass smoothly through zero with no jump and no change in gradient.
walkthrough: Take up the ramp as positive velocity. The ball starts with positive $v$, slows to $v = 0$ at the top, then gains negative $v$ as it rolls back down.
The only force along the ramp, ignoring small rolling friction, is the component of weight down the ramp, so acceleration $a$ is constant and directed down the ramp.
On a velocity-time graph, gradient $= a$. Constant $a$ means the graph must be one straight line with one constant gradient.
Because acceleration is down the ramp while initial velocity is up, the gradient is negative, so the line starts high and falls steadily.
The line crosses the time axis once at the instant $v = 0$ and continues smoothly to negative values with the same slope, showing continuous motion back down. This is option A.

options.A: Single straight line with constant negative gradient crossing from positive to negative velocity shows constant acceleration down the ramp and reversal of direction.
options.B: Velocity stays at zero or positive and returns to zero with changing gradient sign, which would mean speed never reverses direction and acceleration changes sign.
options.C: Sudden vertical jump from positive to negative velocity implies an instantaneous change in velocity at the top, but the ball stops momentarily with $v = 0$.
options.D: Velocity touches zero and then increases positively in a V-shape, which is a speed-time shape and does not show the sign change of vector velocity.
